stances.claim: An incumbent CJ has a responsibility to preside over the orderly transition of power, and the 25-year precedent (1987-2012) shows this can be done seamlessly.
The axiom 'the office must seek the man, not the man seeking the office' protected judicial independence and dignity -- its erosion after 2012 introduced complication and fiasco.

When Miriam Defensor-Santiago applied for the CJ post in 2006, the author declined to respond to her tirade, secure in the conviction that the Court was not ready to be led by an outsider from the political world.
stances.rhetorical_move: first-person autobiographical disclosure with restrained dignity

stances.claim: Sereno's appointment produced three firsts: first woman CJ, first junior justice named chief, first CJ ousted by the Supreme Court via quo warranto.
Aquino frankly told Carpio he could not appoint the most senior justice because of strong objections from his allies -- a candid political fact.
All of CJ Sereno's actions, decisions, and votes are valid under the de facto officer doctrine.
CJ De Castro should restore the precedent by leading the JBC search for her successor now, given only about a month remains in her 42-day term.

notable_anecdotes: The author's own experience as JBC chair in late 2006: Sen. Miriam Defensor-Santiago formally applied for the CJ post, got only 1 JBC vote, and erupted -- 'I am irate. I am foaming at the mouth. I'm homicidal. I'm suicidal. I'm humiliated, degraded... I spit in the face of Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban and his cohorts.' He 'took her tirade in stride and declined to respond in kind.'
President Aquino's frank private conversation with SAJ Carpio during the Sereno selection: admirable decisions and opinions, but cannot appoint him because of strong ally objections.

The Corona succession breaking all precedents: 76 names proposed, 26 accepting, 8 shortlisted (most in JBC history), 3 outsiders shortlisted for the first time, and an eventual 'junior justice' appointed.
CJ De Castro's 42-day tenure -- the shortest in history at the time this column was written -- compared to CJ Pedro Yap's record of 72 days.

decision_framework_signals: Restore the norm: the incumbent CJ should preside over the JBC search for the successor
Treat the 25-year (1987-2012) precedent of insider-only, seniority-weighted nominations as institutional memory worth preserving

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues that an incumbent chief justice has a responsibility to preside over the orderly and smooth transition to a successor -- a norm upheld for 25 years (1987-2012) by all seven CJs from Teehankee through Puno, each leading the Judicial and Bar Council to shortlist three to five insider justices before their mandatory retirements. The precedents broke after Corona's Senate ouster in 2012. He recalls his own chairmanship of the JBC in late 2006, when Sen. Miriam Defensor-Santiago formally applied for his post and, after receiving only one vote, erupted -- 'I am irate... I spit in the face of Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban and his cohorts' -- to which he responded by declining to engage, convinced the Court was not ready for an outsider from the political world. The Corona succession broke every norm: 76 names proposed, 26 accepting, 8 shortlisted (the most ever, including 3 outsiders), and eventually Sereno was chosen -- producing three firsts: first woman CJ, first junior justice named chief, first CJ ousted by the SC via quo warranto. He discloses that Aquino frankly told SAJ Carpio during the selection process that while his decisions were admirable, Aquino could not appoint him because of strong ally objections. He answers queries by reaffirming that all of Sereno's acts as CJ are valid under the de facto officer doctrine. He closes by urging CJ De Castro, with only about a month remaining in her 42-day term, to restore the precedent and lead the JBC search for her successor now.
